label: Göktürk Khaganate
pitch:
The Göktürk Khaganate (552–744 CE) was the first political community in history that called itself Turk. Born from a 552 revolt by the Ashina clan against their Rouran overlords, it grew within twenty years into the largest steppe empire the world had ever seen — stretching from Manchuria to the Caspian, choking the Silk Road, allying with Sasanian Persia to crush the Hephthalites, and sending an embassy to Constantinople to outflank the Sasanians right back. It split into Eastern and Western halves in 582, was crushed by Tang Taizong in 630, came roaring back as the Second Khaganate under Ilterish, and produced the Orkhon Inscriptions — the oldest writing in any Turkic language. When the Uyghurs killed the last khagan in 744, the Turkic peoples fanned out across Eurasia: Karluks, Pechenegs, Seljuks, Ottomans, every modern Turk and every Turkic country traces an ancestral thread back through this dynasty.

🔑 Key Facts:
• Bumin Qaghan founded the empire in 552 by revolting against the Rouran with help from the Sogdians and a marriage alliance with Western Wei China
• At maximum extent (~580) it stretched 4,500 miles from Manchuria to the Black Sea — larger than the contemporary Byzantine and Sasanian empires combined
• Sogdian merchants from Bukhara and Samarkand were the empire's economic spine, running the Silk Road on its behalf
• The Orkhon Inscriptions of 732–735 are the oldest surviving texts in any Turkic language and the oldest first-person royal autobiography from the steppe
• The empire's collapse seeded every later Turkic people from the Khazars on the Volga to the Seljuks in Persia to the Ottomans in Anatolia

🤔 Why It Matters: Every Turkic country today — Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan — and every Turkic-speaking community from the Uyghurs in Xinjiang to the Tatars in Russia traces its ethnonym to the Göktürks. They are the political ancestor of one of the world's largest language families.

🎲 Wild Card: The Sogdian merchant Maniakh led an embassy from the Western Türk court at Suyab all the way to Constantinople in 568, bypassing Sasanian Persia by going north of the Caspian — one of the earliest direct diplomatic contacts between East and West.

spans.label: Steppe Inheritance
spans.description: Before the Türk revolt, the Mongolian steppe passed through a sequence of nomadic powers — the Xianbei (descended from the eastern Donghu), the Rouran Khaganate, and the Hephthalites — each rebuilding the political template the Xiongnu had pioneered. The Ashina clan, blacksmiths and ironworkers in the Altai Mountains, served as Rouran vassals until they were strong enough to revolt.

spans.label: First Türk Khaganate
spans.description: Bumin Qaghan crushed the Rouran in 552 and made the Ashina the masters of the steppe. Within twenty years his brother Istemi had pushed west to the Caspian, allied with Sasanian Persia to destroy the Hephthalites, and then turned the alliance around by opening direct contact with Byzantine Constantinople through Sogdian merchant intermediaries — making the Türks the first steppe empire to play the great-power game across all of Eurasia.

spans.label: East-West Split
spans.description: Civil war between rival branches of the Ashina dynasty fractured the empire into Eastern and Western halves with the Altai Mountains as the rough boundary. The two khaganates fought each other and dealt separately with the rising Sui and then Tang dynasties in China. Tang Taizong's 630 campaign crushed the Eastern Türks, captured the khagan, and made the steppe a Tang protectorate for half a century.

spans.label: Tang Domination
spans.description: Tang Taizong organized the conquered Eastern Türks into a system of subordinate prefectures and proclaimed himself Heavenly Kaghan (Tian Kehan) — the only Chinese emperor in history to hold a steppe imperial title. The Western Türks held on for another generation but were broken between 657 and 659 by the Tang general Su Dingfang, leaving the Tang protectorates of Anxi (Tarim Basin) and Beiting (Dzungaria) in nominal control of the entire Silk Road.

spans.label: Second Türk Khaganate
spans.description: Ilterish Qaghan led a revolt in 682 that drove the Tang out of the Orkhon heartland and re-founded the khaganate. Under his sons Bilge Kagan and Kul Tigin, advised by the elder statesman Tonyukuk, the Second Khaganate reached its peak — and produced the Orkhon Inscriptions, the oldest surviving texts in any Turkic language, in which Bilge addresses his people directly across the centuries.

spans.label: Collapse and Turkic Diaspora
spans.description: In 744 a coalition led by the Uyghurs killed the last Türk khagan and replaced the Ashina with their own dynasty. The displaced Türk clans scattered: the Karluks moved into Transoxiana, the Pechenegs and Bulgars pushed west toward the Black Sea, the Khazars built a Jewish-converting empire on the Volga, and centuries later the Seljuks and then the Ottomans rode out of the Central Asian steppe to take Iran and Anatolia — every one of them a downstream consequence of the Ashina founding.

events.label: Rouran Khaganate
events.description: The nomadic empire that ruled the Mongolian steppe from about 402 to 552, the immediate overlords of the Ashina clan and the first steppe power to call its ruler 'khagan' (great khan). Their destruction by their own blacksmith vassals opened the way for the Türks.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Rouran founder, Yujiulü Shelun, started life as a slave of the Xianbei before unifying the steppe and adopting the khagan title around 402. Chinese sources of the period sneer at the Rouran with the name 'Ruru,' a deliberately insulting term meaning roughly 'wriggling insects.' Their dynastic story has a neat symmetry with the Türks': just as the Rouran began as somebody else's slaves, they ended at the hands of their own slave-caste blacksmiths.

events.label: Hephthalite Empire
events.description: The Hephthalites, the 'White Huns' of Greek and Persian writers, ran a sprawling Central Asian empire from roughly 450 to 560 CE — straddling Sogdiana, Bactria, parts of India, and the central Silk Road that everybody else wanted.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: They had Persia by the throat for decades: from 474 the Sasanians paid them tribute, and after Shah Peroz I marched out for a third try and got killed near Balkh in 484, the Persian state basically became a Hephthalite client for about fifty years. The 'White Hun' label is a Greek and Persian convention, not a proven family tie to Attila's Huns. Their kings are murky figures — one of the better-attested is Khingila, known mostly from coins, which is how a lot of Hephthalite history survives at all.

events.label: The Ashina Clan
events.description: The founding royal clan of the Türks, whose name means 'Noble Wolf.' Chinese chroniclers describe them as a small ironworking caste embedded in the Rouran empire, mining and smelting in the Altai before they rose to rule the steppe.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Scholars still argue over where the Ashina actually came from before they show up as Rouran subjects — proposals range from a Xiongnu splinter group to refugees from Gansu in northwest China who fled to the Altai around 460. The clan name has been traced by some linguists not to Turkic at all but to an Eastern Iranian word for 'blue' (the same color sense behind 'Göktürk,' literally 'Blue/Celestial Türk'). The Ashina bloodline became so prestigious that for centuries afterward, far-flung Turkic dynasties claimed descent from it the way European kings later claimed descent from Charlemagne.

events.label: The She-Wolf Founding Myth
events.description: The Türk origin story, written down by Chinese chroniclers from Türk oral tradition: a boy is the lone survivor of a massacre, a she-wolf nurses him and bears his ten sons, and the eldest line becomes the Ashina royal house. The wolf became the dynasty's emblem.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The fullest version survives in the Book of Zhou, a seventh-century Chinese history — in it the wolf, pregnant and pursued, crosses a sea to a cave in the mountains northwest of Gaochang (an oasis city near modern Turpan in northwest China) to give birth. Chinese sources actually preserve a competing origin legend too, in which the founding ancestor descends from a summer and winter spirit rather than a wolf, a reminder that the Türks themselves told more than one story about where they came from. The grey wolf endured as a Turkic symbol for well over a thousand years and was deliberately revived by twentieth-century Turkish nationalists.

events.label: Ashina Iron-Working in the Altai
events.description: Before they were rulers, the Ashina were miners and smiths, digging iron out of the southern Altai Mountains and paying their Rouran overlords in finished weapons. This metalworking trade — not yet their cavalry — was the foundation of their early reputation and wealth.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Türk oral tradition kept the memory of the forge alive long after the clan became emperors: each year the khagan and his nobles held a ceremony in which they ritually hammered a piece of iron, re-enacting the smithing origins of the dynasty. Iron in the sixth-century steppe was scarce and precious, which made a tribe that controlled its production into a strategic supplier the way an oil state is today. The Altai range itself takes its name from a Mongolic-Turkic root meaning 'golden,' and it remained one of Inner Asia's richest mining zones for metals long after the Türks were gone.

events.label: Bumin Qaghan
events.description: The founder of the Türk empire. In 552 he smashed the Rouran, took the supreme title, and married into a Chinese royal house to seal an alliance — then died within months, before he could rule the state he had just created.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The title Bumin took on was 'Illig Qaghan,' which means roughly 'ruler of the people' in Old Turkic. His path to the throne ran through a Chinese bride: the Western Wei court sent him Princess Changle in the summer of 551, a match that lent him semi-imperial standing by Chinese diplomatic convention. The dynasty he founded outlasted him by a century and a half and seeded later branches stretching from Mongolia to the Black Sea, even though he personally sat on the throne for only a few months.

events.label: Revolt Against the Rouran
events.description: Bumin's 552 uprising. His cavalry crushed the Rouran field army, the last Rouran khagan killed himself, and the blacksmith vassals became the new masters of the steppe — with the broken Rouran fleeing west toward Europe.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The revolt was set up by an earlier favor that exposed how strong the Ashina had quietly become: Bumin had crushed a rebellion of the Tiele tribes and absorbed the surrender of more than 50,000 households, then felt powerful enough to demand a Rouran princess as his wife. The khagan Anagui refused with a famous insult, calling Bumin his 'blacksmith slave' — the line Chinese chroniclers preserved word for word. The decisive battle was fought near Huaihuang, in the area of modern Zhangjiakou in Hebei province, just northwest of Beijing.

events.label: The Title Qaghan
events.description: The imperial title 'qaghan' (great khan), which Bumin adopted in 552, went on to become the standard name for supreme rulers across Inner Asia for the next thousand years — the word behind everything from Genghis Khan to the khans of Crimea.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The title wasn't actually a Türk invention or even a Rouran one: it appears to trace back further still to Xianbei nobility, and the Rouran founder Shelun was simply the first to apply it systematically to a supreme steppe ruler around 402. It coexisted for a while with the much older Xiongnu term 'chanyu' before displacing it entirely. The word's reach is enormous — the modern Turkish, Mongolian, and many Central Asian languages still carry descendants of 'khagan,' and it even worked its way into Russian and other European languages through medieval contact with the steppe.

events.label: The Orkhon Valley Heartland
events.description: The broad upland river basin in central Mongolia where the khagan pitched his summer camp and held the great annual assembly — the geographic heart of the new empire, sheltered by mountains, with reliable water and good grass for the horse herds.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The valley was such a magnet for steppe power that it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004 precisely for stacking two thousand years of nomadic capitals in one place: the Türks' camp, the Uyghur city of Ordu-Baliq (which sprawled across roughly 19 square miles, or 50 sq km), and Genghis Khan's Karakorum, founded in 1220. The protected landscape today covers about 470 square miles (1,220 sq km) of pasture along both banks of the river. Later rulers kept returning to the exact same ground partly to borrow the legitimacy of whoever had ruled there before.

events.label: Istemi Yabghu and the Western Empire
events.description: Bumin's younger brother and the engineer of the Türks' western expansion. As 'yabghu' (junior khan of the western wing) he drove the frontier across Central Asia, partnered with Persia to destroy the Hephthalites, and opened direct relations with Constantinople.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Istemi and the Sasanian shah Khosrow I jointly crushed the Hephthalites (a powerful Central Asian power sometimes called the 'White Huns') by about 560, then promptly fell out over who controlled the silk trade through the lands between them. Blocked by Persia, Istemi was talked by a Sogdian merchant-diplomat named Maniakh into going over Persia's head entirely: a Türk embassy reached the Byzantine emperor Justin II in Constantinople in 568, offering silk and a joint alliance against Persia. It was the first direct diplomatic contact between a steppe empire and Byzantium, and it stitched the Türk khaganate into the politics of the whole Eurasian world.

events.label: Sasanian-Türk Alliance
events.description: Around 557-558 Istemi cut a deal with the Sasanian shah Khusrau I to gang up on the Hephthalites — Persians hitting from the south, Türks from the north, the enemy crushed in between.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Khusrau I (reigned 531-579) was the dynasty's heavyweight, remembered in Persian tradition by the epithet Anushirvan ('the immortal soul') for his tax and army reforms. The alliance wasn't just a handshake: it was sealed by marriage, with Khusrau taking a daughter of the Türk khagan as a wife. Persia had a century-old grudge to settle here, having paid the Hephthalites tribute since the 470s, so for Khusrau this was less a fresh war than a long-overdue reckoning.

events.label: Destruction of the Hephthalites
events.description: The joint Sasanian-Türk attack of 557-560 finished the Hephthalites off, ending more than a century of their grip on Sogdiana and the central Silk Road, with the Oxus River left as the rough boundary between the two victors.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The decisive clash is usually called the Battle of Gol-Zarriun (or of Bukhara), fought near Bukhara in modern Uzbekistan around 560; the Hephthalite king — named Gatfar in later Persian tradition — was beaten and the army shattered. The empire didn't vanish so much as splinter into a scatter of small principalities that lingered as Sasanian or Türk vassals. Splitting the spoils at the Oxus planted the seed of the next war: within a decade the two allies were squabbling over who really controlled the river towns and their silk trade.

events.label: Sogdian Merchant Diaspora
events.description: The Sogdians were an Iranian-speaking trading people from the oases of modern Uzbekistan and Tajikistan who became the merchant class, diplomats, and first scribes of the Türk Empire. Their family-run colonies and shared Sogdian language strung together a commercial web that ran from Constantinople to the Chinese capital.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The oldest writing we have in Sogdian is a bundle of five letters known as the "Ancient Letters," found in 1907 by archaeologist Aurel Stein stuffed in a ruined watchtower near Dunhuang in western China. They date to around 313 CE — over two centuries before the Türks arrived — and read like a snapshot of the network in action: one, written by a merchant named Nanai-vandak to his "home office" back in Samarkand, talks shop about silk, musk, silver, and slaves. The mailbag they came from seems to have been lost or seized in transit, which is why they sat unread for sixteen hundred years.

events.label: Türk Control of the Silk Road
events.description: Having broken the Hephthalites, the Türks held the central Silk Road from the Tarim Basin to the Caspian, with Sogdian merchants as their commercial agents. That made the khaganate the toll-keeper between China, Persia, India, and Byzantium — wildly profitable, and an instant source of friction with Persia.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The romantic phrase "Silk Road" is much younger than the road itself — it was coined in 1877 by a German geographer-explorer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, who wrote it in German as "Seidenstraße" (uncle, incidentally, of the World War I flying ace the "Red Baron"). The Türks and Sogdians never called it anything of the kind. The label only caught on with the wider public in the 20th century, long after the trade it described had faded.

events.label: Bukhara and Samarkand
events.description: Bukhara and Samarkand were the two great Sogdian oasis cities of Transoxiana, the irrigated belt between the Oxus and Jaxartes rivers. Under Türk overlordship from the 560s, they were the commercial and intellectual anchors of the empire's western half before later becoming famous Islamic-world capitals.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Both cities are staggeringly old. The oldest core of Samarkand, the mound now called Afrasiyab, was settled around the 7th century BCE and stayed occupied for nearly two thousand years until Genghis Khan's armies wrecked it in 1220. Bukhara's official founding is pegged to roughly 500 BCE, when scattered settlements in the oasis had grown together behind a single wall. That depth is why these two kept reinventing themselves as capitals — first for the Sogdians, then for the Persian Samanids, and later (for Samarkand) for Timur's empire.

events.label: Persian Silk Embargo
events.description: Sasanian shah Khusrau I shut Sogdian silk out of Persian markets to protect Persia's own royal silk monopoly, then humiliated the Türk envoys who came to negotiate. The quarrel turned two recent allies hostile and pushed the Türks to look west, toward Byzantium, for a buyer.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Our source for this is the Byzantine historian Menander Protector, and the snub came in two ugly stages. According to him, when the first Türk-Sogdian embassy arrived, the Persians bought the silk they brought and then burned it in front of them to make a point that they didn't actually want it. When a second embassy came, the Sasanians poisoned the envoys outright. It was the Sogdian merchant Maniakh who reportedly talked the khagan Istemi out of war and into the audacious end-run to Constantinople instead.

events.label: Maniakh's Byzantine Embassy
events.description: In 568 a Sogdian merchant named Maniakh led a Türk embassy all the way from Istemi's court to Constantinople, looping north of the Caspian to dodge hostile Persia and pitch a direct silk-and-alliance deal to the Byzantines.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Maniakh wasn't a random courier — Byzantine sources call him 'chief of the people of Sogdiana,' and it was his idea to approach Rome in the first place, since Sogdian traders were the ones losing money when Persia slammed its markets shut. The embassy showed up bearing raw silk as a gift, and Justin II quizzed Maniakh personally about the Türks and their lands. The whole episode survives because the Byzantine official Menander Protector copied long extracts of the diplomatic record into his history, written around 580.

events.label: Zemarchus's Embassy to the Türks
events.description: To ratify the deal Maniakh had opened, Justin II sent the diplomat Zemarchus of Cilicia east in 569, traveling back with the Türk embassy to Istemi's court — and his report is the earliest detailed Western eyewitness account of the steppe khaganate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Menander dates the departure precisely: Zemarchus left Constantinople in August 569. He found the khagan encamped in a mountain valley the Greeks rendered as 'Ektag,' or Golden Mountain, somewhere in the Tian Shan range. Istemi received him seated on a golden throne inside a felt tent hung with colored silks, surrounded by his guard and his Sogdian advisers. The return leg was its own ordeal — Zemarchus's party had to slip back across the Caucasus while dodging Persian forces who'd gotten wind of the new alliance.

events.label: Dual Kingship System
events.description: The khaganate ran on two thrones at once: a senior khagan in the Mongolian east and a junior 'yabghu' running the Central Asian west as a near-equal co-ruler with his own court, armies, and foreign policy. Brilliant for covering a continent; a time bomb at every succession.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The design let one wing handle China while the other handled Persia and Byzantium thousands of miles away without either ruler having to split his attention. It worked as long as a single generation held both halves and everyone agreed who was senior. When cousins began fighting over which branch of the ruling Ashina clan outranked the other, the whole structure split apart — which is exactly what happened in 582, breaking the empire into eastern and western halves that never reunited.

events.label: Tengri Sky Worship
events.description: The Türks worshipped Tengri, the eternal blue sky — the same supreme deity the Xiongnu, Xianbei, and later Mongols all venerated. The khagan ruled by the 'mandate of Tengri' (kut), a concept that paralleled the Chinese Mandate of Heaven and was probably influenced by it. Türk religious specialists called kam (the source of the English word 'shaman' via Tungusic languages) communicated with Tengri and the spirits through trance, drum, and animal sacrifice.

events.label: Muqan Qaghan
events.description: Bumin's son and the warrior-administrator who turned a year-old founding into a continental empire (553–572), conquering the steppe's eastern margins and squeezing tribute out of a divided China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Muqan's armies finished crushing the Rouran (the people the Türks had overthrown) by around 555, routed the Khitan to the east, and annexed the Yenisei Kyrgyz to the north. In 557 the Türks smashed the Hephthalites near Bukhara in a pincer alliance with the Sasanian Persian king Khosrow I — though that western campaign was really run by Muqan's uncle Istemi, who commanded the empire's western wing. When Muqan died in 572 the throne passed not to a son but to his younger brother Taspar, following the steppe habit of passing power across a generation of brothers before dropping to the next.

events.label: Silk Tribute from Chinese States
events.description: With the Chinese north split between two warring dynasties, Muqan played both sides — each bought his neutrality with silk, and neither could afford to be the one who stopped paying.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chinese records put the figure at 100,000 bolts of silk a year, the heaviest tribute China had handed the steppe since the Han dynasty's marriage-alliance treaties some seven centuries earlier (though sources differ on whether that number was per state or the combined haul from both). The silk barely paused in the khagan's tents before flowing west through Sogdian merchants into Persian and Byzantine markets, which is what made it so valuable — it was less a hoard than working capital. When the Sui dynasty reunified China in 589 and the payments dried up, the Türks were left with a sudden hole in their finances.

events.label: Tardu Yabghu
events.description: Tardu was the long-ruling western yabghu (sub-khan) and a son of Istemi, the brother who had built the empire's western wing. In 599 he made a grab to reunite both halves under himself as sole 'great khagan,' but the bid fell apart by 603 when his own subject tribes revolted, egged on by Chinese diplomacy, and he vanished from the record.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tribes who broke Tardu were the Tiele (his nomadic vassals), a coalition that included the Uyghurs and the Xueyantuo — peoples who would loom large in steppe history for centuries after. The Sui court didn't fight Tardu so much as quietly fund his enemies into rebellion, a cheaper and more reliable weapon than any army. After his subjects turned on him around 603 or 604 he simply disappeared and was probably killed; the histories don't even give him a death scene.

events.label: East-West Split
events.description: When Taspar Qaghan died in 581 the empire had no clear heir, so rival branches of the ruling Ashina family fought a civil war over the throne. By 582 the realm had cracked into an Eastern Khaganate (the Mongolian heartland) and a Western one (the Tian Shan, Sogdiana, and the steppes north of the Caspian), roughly divided at the Altai Mountains, and the two halves never reunited.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The trigger was a contested will. Taspar wanted the throne to go to Apa Qaghan, but the high council threw out his wishes — partly on the grounds that Apa's mother was not of Türk blood — and installed Ishbara instead. There were really four men with claims (a son, two nephews, and a cousin, Tardu, out west), and the losers simply set up their own courts in their own territories, so the 'split' was less a clean break than a map that nobody could agree on. The eastern khagan ruled from the sacred Ötüken forest in central Mongolia, the spiritual center of steppe power.

events.label: Sui Reunification of China
events.description: In 589 the Sui Dynasty finished stitching China back together for the first time since the Han collapse in 220, ending nearly four centuries of division. The reunified Sui was richer, more populous, and far more aggressive than the squabbling northern dynasties that had been paying the Türks protection money — and it promptly turned that new muscle against the steppe, bankrolling rival khagans to fight each other.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The conquest of the southern Chen Dynasty was fast and overwhelming: the Sui massed somewhere around 500,000 troops along the Yangtze, and the southern capital Jiankang (modern Nanjing) fell in roughly four months. The dynasty had been founded in 581 by Yang Jian (Emperor Wen), who had been the power-behind-the-throne regent for the Northern Zhou before taking the crown himself. For all its might the Sui burned out fast — it lasted under forty years before collapsing in 618, making it one of the shortest-lived major dynasties in Chinese history.

events.label: Shibi Qaghan Surrounds the Sui Emperor
events.description: In 615 the Eastern Türk khagan Shibi caught the Sui emperor Yang Guang touring the northern frontier and pinned him inside a small walled town at Yanmen Pass for over a month — a deliberate echo of the Xiongnu's famous humiliation of the Han founder eight centuries before. The emperor escaped, but the loss of face helped tip the dynasty into the rebellions that destroyed it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Shibi turned hostile because a Sui official, Pei Ju, had lured the khagan's chief strategist to a meeting and murdered him — so the siege was partly revenge. What actually lifted it was a clever ruse, not a battle: the emperor smuggled an appeal to Princess Yicheng, a Sui royal woman married off to Shibi, who was running affairs back at the Türk capital. She sent her husband a false report that the Türks were under attack from the north, and Shibi broke off the siege to rush home. That same princess turns up again, fatally, fifteen years later.

events.label: Tang Dynasty Founded with Türk Help
events.description: Li Yuan, the Sui frontier governor who launched the revolt that became the Tang Dynasty in 618, kicked things off by paying tribute to the Eastern Türk khagan Shibi and accepting nominal Türk overlordship — buying cavalry and a promise that the Türks wouldn't stab him in the back as he marched on the capital. It was a humiliating bargain the Tang would spend the next decade trying to erase.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Türks were partly conned into the deal: a carefully worded letter let Shibi believe Li Yuan meant to make the new Chinese state a Türk vassal, and in exchange the Türks handed over 2,000 horses and 500 soldiers. Li Yuan was famously pushed into rebelling by his ambitious second son, Li Shimin — the same son who would later seize the throne by killing his brothers. Li Yuan ruled as Emperor Gaozu until 626, when that son forced him to abdicate.

events.label: Illig Qaghan
events.description: Illig (called Xieli in Chinese sources) was the last khagan of the Eastern Türks, and his reign ended in slow-motion disaster. A brutal snowstorm around 627 killed off his herds, and when he tried to squeeze replacement horses out of his vassal tribes they revolted instead — leaving him fatally weakened just as a vengeful Tang emperor was looking for an opening.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Early on, Illig had the upper hand: in 626, only days after Tang Taizong took the throne, Türk armies rode right up to the Wei River across from the capital Chang'an, and the new emperor had to ride out and personally buy them off with tribute at what's remembered as the alliance at the Bian Bridge — a humiliation he never forgot. The tribes who broke Illig after the great winter were the Tiele, led by a Xueyantuo coalition. After his final defeat in 630 he was run down, captured, and shipped to Chang'an, where he lived out his days as a prisoner of the court.

events.label: Tang Conquest of the Eastern Türks
events.description: In early 630 the Tang general Li Jing drove a winter campaign across the frozen north and stormed the Eastern Türk khagan Illig in his own camp. The Türk army was shattered, the khagan was run down and captured, and within weeks the Eastern Türk Khaganate simply stopped existing — its tribes resettled in the Ordos loop as Tang military auxiliaries.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The killing blow came at the Battle of Yinshan on March 27, 630, near modern Hohhot in Inner Mongolia. Li Jing's vanguard — led by Su Dingfang, who would later go on to crush the Western Türks — fell on the khagan's camp while Illig was stalling with fake peace offers, his men carrying only about twenty days of supplies so they could move fast and light. Among the dead was Princess Yicheng, the Sui royal woman who had saved an emperor with a lie at Yanmen in 615; by 630 she had married into the Türk khagans, and the Tang put her to death after the victory.

events.label: Tang Taizong as Heavenly Kaghan
events.description: After crushing the Türks in 630, the surrendered steppe leaders proclaimed Tang Taizong 'Tian Kehan' (Heavenly Khan) — the only Chinese emperor ever to formally carry a steppe imperial title. He now held two crowns at once: Son of Heaven over the settled Chinese world and Heavenly Khan over the nomads, notionally the supreme ruler of both halves of Eurasia.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The title was a genuine hybrid — 'Tian' is the Chinese word for heaven, while 'Kehan' is just the Chinese spelling-out of the steppe word khagan, so the name itself fused the two traditions in three syllables. The histories first record him being hailed this way on May 20, 630, only weeks after Illig's capture. The arrangement was never turned into a permanent institution, but the cosmopolitan flavor it gave the Tang — a court comfortable with Turks, Sogdians, and steppe custom — became one of the dynasty's defining traits.

events.label: Anxi Protectorate
events.description: The Anxi Protectorate (an-SHEE, "Pacifying the West") was the Tang command post that ran the Tarim Basin and the Silk Road, founded in 640 at Gaochang and built around a ring of garrison towns.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The headquarters moved twice: it started at Gaochang (modern Turfan) in 640 and shifted to Kucha in 648 once the Tang took that oasis. The famous Four Garrisons were installed piecemeal between 648 and 658, not all at once. At its 659 high-water mark the protectorate collected nominal submissions from places as far west as Samarkand, Bukhara, Tashkent, and Kabul. The whole structure outlasted the dynasty's grip on the region for over a century before finally falling to Tibet around 790.

events.label: Western Türk Collapse
events.description: The Western Türks outlasted their eastern cousins by a generation, but once the Tang were done in the east they turned west. General Su Dingfang's campaign of 657-659 broke the Western Khaganate and brought down its last khagan, Ashina Helu, ending more than a century of Ashina rule over Central Asia.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The decisive clash was the Battle of the Irtysh River near the Altai Mountains in 657, where Helu's 100,000 horsemen charged Su Dingfang's infantry three times and were repulsed each time before Tang cavalry sprang an ambush from behind a hill; Helu fled and was run down and captured the following day. The win let the Tang bolt the region into its administrative grid through the Anxi Protectorate, which governed the Silk Road oasis cities of the Tarim Basin (Kashgar, Khotan, Kucha, and others). At its height the Tang frontier now reached deep into Central Asia, the high-water mark of Chinese westward power.

events.label: Tang Reach Maximum in Central Asia
events.description: By around 660 the Tang Empire reached its territorial maximum, stretching from the Pacific coast all the way to the edge of Central Asia — the largest the Chinese empire would be for roughly a thousand years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: That western reach stopped for good ninety years later at the Battle of Talas (751), where a Tang army under the Korean-born general Gao Xianzhi was beaten by the Abbasid Caliphate and its Karluk allies near the Talas River. The defeat ended Chinese expansion west of the Pamirs permanently. By tradition, Chinese papermakers captured at Talas passed the craft to the Islamic world — a tidy story historians treat with some caution, but papermaking did spread westward from there. Four years later the An Lushan Rebellion gutted the Tang and forced it to abandon Central Asia altogether.

events.label: Ilterish Qaghan
events.description: The junior Ashina noble Kutlugh, a Tang frontier officer, broke away in 682, gathered a tiny band of Türk loyalists, and within three years had thrown the Tang out of the Mongolian steppe and rebuilt the khaganate. He took the throne name Ilterish ("the Gatherer") and ruled until his death in 691.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Kutlugh was a grandson of Illig Qaghan, the last ruler of the First Khaganate that the Tang had crushed back in 630, so his revolt was a family score-settling as much as a national one. The Tonyukuk Inscription gives the founding force as just seventeen men, swelling to seven hundred once Tonyukuk threw in with him, and only then into a real army. His personal name Qutlugh literally means "blessed with good fortune," which is roughly the steppe equivalent of being named "Lucky."

events.label: Türk Revolt of 682
events.description: In 682 a junior Ashina noble named Kutlugh broke away from Tang service and re-founded an independent Türk khaganate, taking the throne name Ilterish ("the One Who Gathered the People"). It was the spark that became the Second Türk Khaganate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The legend that he started with just seventeen men is roughly how the Chinese sources tell it — that handful grew to around seven hundred, and he based himself at Black Sand City north of modern Hohhot. His secret weapon was the brilliant statesman Tonyukuk, a Türk raised and educated in China who became his chief strategist and whose own stone memorial still stands in Mongolia. After consolidating, Ilterish turned in 687 to conquer the old Türk heartland on the Orkhon, crushing the Toquz Oghuz and Uyghurs who held it. He died in 692, and his brother Qapaghan took over.

events.label: Tonyukuk
events.description: Tonyukuk (TON-yoo-kook) was the elder statesman who served as chief minister to a string of Second Khaganate rulers across roughly forty years. Tang-raised and fluent in Chinese, he brought the new state working knowledge of how settled empires governed, and his own inscription is the oldest first-person testimony from any steppe culture.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By his own inscription he had escaped Tang captivity in 681 to join Ilterish's revolt the next year, and his stele names him as counselor to four khagans (Ilterish, Kapaghan, the short-lived Inel, and Bilge), not three. He raised the monument himself around 716, while still alive, in the Tuul (Tula) River basin near present-day Ulaanbaatar. A Chinese record claims he lived to 120 years old, which is almost certainly an admiring exaggeration but tells you how legendary his longevity already seemed.

events.label: Kapaghan Qaghan
events.description: Kapaghan Qaghan (called Mochuo in Chinese), Ilterish's brother, ruled from 691 to 716 and pushed the khaganate to its military peak — beating the Khitan and Kyrgyz, raiding deep into China, and at one point forcing the Tang court to sue for peace. His harsh, suspicious final years bred revolt, and he was killed in an ambush in 716.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He was ambushed and beheaded on 22 July 716 by a man of the Bayegu (Bayirku) tribe while riding through a forest after a campaign against the Toquz Oghuz tribal alliance. His severed head was carried south and displayed at the Tang capital Chang'an as a trophy. The humiliating treaty he had earlier wrung from the Tang came while Wu Zetian sat on the throne under her own Zhou dynasty, the only time a woman ruled China in her own name.

events.label: Bilge Kagan
events.description: Bilge Kagan (BIL-geh, "the Wise") ruled the Second Khaganate from 716 to 734, the son of its founder Ilterish and brother of the warrior Kul Tigin. His reign was unusually peaceful and prosperous, and the speeches he had carved into the Orkhon stones are the oldest surviving first-person voice of any steppe ruler.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He died on 25 November 734, poisoned over several days by his own minister Buyruq Chor, but lingered long enough to have the killer and his entire clan put to death first; his funeral was held the following June. Despite the narrative's friendly trade ties, Bilge never actually landed the Tang princess he chased — Emperor Xuanzong strung the negotiations along with delays and excuses and the marriage was still unsettled when Bilge was poisoned. His own funerary stele, raised in 735, is the longest and most complete Türk account of the whole khaganate.

events.label: Kul Tigin
events.description: Kul Tigin was Bilge Kagan's younger brother and the war leader of the Second Khaganate. After Kapaghan's death in 716 he led a night raid that wiped out the rival claimant and put his own brother on the throne. He died in 731, and the great inscription Bilge raised over his grave is one of the three Orkhon monuments.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He was born in 684 and died suddenly on 27 February 731, with his elaborate burial held that 1 November. As a young commander he fought at the brutal Battle of Bolchu in 711, where Tonyukuk and Kul Tigin smashed a rebel coalition reckoned at around a hundred thousand men. The memorial stele Bilge built for him in 732 carries text in both Old Turkic and Chinese, and the Tang emperor Xuanzong actually sent his own artisans north to carve and decorate the tomb.

events.label: The Orkhon Inscriptions
events.description: The three Orkhon Inscriptions — Tonyukuk's (raised ~716), Kul Tigin's (732), and Bilge Kagan's (735) — are the oldest surviving texts in any Turkic language. Carved in the Old Turkic runiform script in central Mongolia's Orkhon Valley, they preserve the rulers' own voices and read like steppe political philosophy in stone.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The stones lay unread for over a thousand years until a Russian expedition under Nikolai Yadrintsev rediscovered them in 1889, and the Danish philologist Vilhelm Thomsen cracked the script on 15 December 1893, reportedly identifying the words for "Türk" and "Tengri" first. The Kul Tigin and Bilge monuments stand only about a kilometer apart at the site now called Khöshöö-Tsaidam. Each was far more than a single slab: the steles sat inside walled funerary complexes with statues, offering altars, and rows of stone figures.

events.label: Old Turkic Script
events.description: The Old Turkic script (also called the Orkhon script) is the angular alphabet used to carve the inscriptions — the first writing system custom-built for a Turkic language. It almost certainly descends from a non-cursive form of the Sogdian alphabet, reshaped to fit Turkic sounds; its runelike look is pure coincidence.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It runs to roughly 38 characters and was normally written from right to left, with some inscriptions stacked vertically instead. Many of its vowels go unwritten, left to be inferred through vowel harmony (a feature of Turkic where the vowels in a word all belong to the same front-or-back group). When Vilhelm Thomsen first published it he simply called the letters "Turkish runes," a nickname that stuck even though the script has no real link to the runes of Germanic Europe.

events.label: Bilge's Warning Against Sinicization
events.description: The most quoted passage of the Orkhon Inscriptions is Bilge Kagan's blunt warning to his people not to be seduced by Chinese silk, gold, titles, and walled cities — to stay in the Otüken heartland and take what they needed through trade, never letting the court drift south. It is the earliest articulate steppe critique of being absorbed by a settled neighbor.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Otüken, the homeland Bilge tells his people never to leave, refers to the sacred forested highlands of the Khangai-Orkhon region in central Mongolia, long regarded as the spiritual seat of steppe sovereignty. The argument was not entirely original — Tonyukuk's older inscription had already made the same case against settling down. What makes Bilge's version land harder is that he frames China's gifts as a deliberate trap: corrupt one leader with "sweet words," he says, and through that one man you corrupt his whole people.

events.label: Poisoning of Bilge Kagan
events.description: In 734 Bilge Kagan was poisoned by his own minister Buyruq Chor, dying slowly enough to have the murderer and his entire clan exterminated before he himself died. His death stripped the khaganate of its one stabilizing figure, and within a decade the Türk state had collapsed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He died on 25 November 734 and was buried the next summer, on 22 June 735, the same year his great memorial stele went up. The poisoning came right after he had sent yet another embassy to the Tang emperor Xuanzong angling for a marriage alliance, fueling old speculation that Chinese intrigue may have had a hand in it. The weak khagans who scrambled for his throne could not hold the confederation together, and by 742 the subject Uyghurs, Karluks, and Basmyls were in open revolt.

events.label: Uyghur-Karluk-Basmyl Coalition
events.description: In 742 three subject peoples — the Uyghurs, Karluks, and Basmyls — joined forces and rose against their Ashina (the Türk royal clan) overlords, killing one khagan and then his successor by 744. The Uyghur chief Kutluk Bilge claimed the imperial title, and the Türk state was finished.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The coalition was a temporary marriage of convenience that fell apart almost immediately: once the Ashina were gone, the three allies turned on each other. The Basmyls had briefly installed their own leader as khagan, but the Uyghurs and Karluks then crushed the Basmyls and split the spoils, with the Uyghurs taking the Mongolian heartland and the Karluks heading west. So the rebellion that ended one empire instantly triggered a three-way scramble to inherit it.

events.label: Uyghur Khaganate
events.description: Founded in 744 on the wreckage of the Türk state, the Uyghur Khaganate ran the Mongolian steppe for nearly a century. Unlike the nomadic Türks, the Uyghurs adopted the Persian religion Manichaeism and built a real walled capital — until a Kyrgyz invasion wiped them out in 840.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Their khagan Bögü is reckoned the first ruler anywhere to make Manichaeism (a dualist faith of light-versus-dark founded by the third-century prophet Mani) a state religion, and the religion's headquarters in Mesopotamia thought enough of him to send senior clergy out to Mongolia. The capital, Ordu-Baliq (also called Karabalghasun), sprawled over an estimated 15 square miles (40 sq km) with an 80-foot-wide main avenue and a roughly 40-foot (13 m) stupa-like mound — astonishing for a people the Chinese still pictured as tent-dwellers. The end came fast: the savage winter of 839–840 killed off the herds, and a famine-weakened Uyghur state was overrun by about 80,000 Kyrgyz horsemen who razed the city.

events.label: Karluk Migration West
events.description: After the collapse the Karluks, one of the rebel tribes, drifted southwest into the Ili River valley and on toward Transoxiana (the land beyond the Oxus River, roughly modern Uzbekistan). There they would eventually build the Karakhanid state — and along the way they tipped the Battle of Talas by switching sides mid-fight.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Karluks' real claim to fame came in the tenth century: their Karakhanid dynasty was the first Turkic ruling house to adopt Islam, under a khan remembered as Satuq Bughra Khan, and it became the first Turkic-Muslim state to make a written literary language of its own. One of its court figures, Mahmud al-Kashgari, compiled the first great dictionary of the Turkic tongues (the 'Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk', around 1077) — meaning these former herders produced the earliest serious scholarship about the Turkic languages themselves.

events.label: Battle of Talas
events.description: In July 751 an Abbasid Arab army beat a Tang Chinese army by the Talas River in what is now Kyrgyzstan, halting China's push west and steering Central Asia toward Islam. The Karluk auxiliaries flipped from the Chinese to the Arab side partway through the fight, and the Tang army fell apart.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The famous story that Chinese prisoners taken here taught papermaking to the Islamic world — supposedly spreading it from Samarkand to Baghdad — is almost certainly a later legend; archaeologists have found paper in Samarkand from before 751, so the technology was already there. The defeated Tang general, Gao Xianzhi, was Korean-born and had earlier pulled off a daring high-altitude crossing of the Pamir mountains, but Talas ended his run; he was executed a few years later during the chaos of the An Lushan Rebellion. Tang military power never returned to the region.

events.label: Arab Conquest of Transoxiana
events.description: Between 705 and 715 the Umayyad general Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered the Sogdian oases of Bukhara, Samarkand, Khwarezm, and Ferghana, ending more than a century of Türk overlordship over the western Silk Road. The conquest brought Islam into Sogdian territory and effectively closed the Western Türk legacy in Central Asia, even though the Tang nominally still claimed the region.

events.label: Kumis and Steppe Drinking Culture
events.description: Kumis (KOO-mis) — fermented mare's milk, tart and mildly boozy — was the steppe's signature drink, and Türk feasts that swam in it were a working part of court politics, with Zemarchus's embassy plied with the stuff at Istemi's court.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The kick is real but gentle: mare's milk carries more sugar than cow's or goat's, so ordinary kumis ferments to around 3 percent alcohol — less than most beer. The drink is ancient — Herodotus described Scythians churning mare's milk in wooden buckets back in the fifth century BCE, and Han-era Chinese borrowed both the product and a word for it from the Xiongnu. The Turkic name itself (qımız) first shows up in writing in Mahmud al-Kashgari's eleventh-century dictionary of Turkic languages, and Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, and Mongols still drink it today.

events.label: Türk Iron Stirrup Cavalry
events.description: The Türks made the iron stirrup standard kit for their riders, giving each warrior a stable footing to fire a bow or drive a lance from the saddle. They didn't invent it, but they were the people who turned it into a battlefield system — and then exported it west.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The oldest paired riding stirrups archaeologists have found come from Xianbei tombs in northeastern China, with images of them dating to around 322 CE, more than two centuries before the Türks rose. The technology reached Europe through the Avars: the earliest stirrups in European ground come from sixth-century Avar graves in present-day Hungary. Once Frankish and other Western knights adopted it, the stirrup let a rider couch a lance firmly under his arm and put the full charging weight of horse and man behind the point — the move that made the armored medieval knight possible and ruled European battlefields for centuries.

events.label: Türk Composite Bow
events.description: The Türks inherited and refined the composite bow tradition of the Xiongnu and Xianbei: a recurve bow built from horn, sinew, and wood, glued together over months and capable of shooting an arrow accurately at over 200 yards from horseback. Combined with the iron stirrup, the composite bow gave Türk cavalry a tactical advantage over almost every settled army they faced.

events.label: Türk Felt Tents and Wagon Camps
events.description: The Türks lived in round felt tents (the same structure later called ger by Mongols and yurt by Turks) carried on ox-drawn carts. Khagans traveled with massive wagon camps that could be set up as walled fortresses by parking the carts in a defensive ring — a technique that the Mongols would later adapt and that medieval Europeans called a 'wagon laager.' Zemarchus's embassy described Istemi's gold-cloth-covered ceremonial tent in admiring detail.

events.label: An Lushan Rebellion and Türk Diaspora
events.description: The An Lushan Rebellion of 755–763 nearly toppled the Tang Dynasty and was led by a general of mixed Sogdian-Türk parentage from the old western frontier. Its aftermath shattered Tang control of the frontier, pulled Chinese power out of Central Asia, and left the Turkic peoples free to chart their own course.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It ranks among the deadliest events in all of history: Tang census rolls fell from roughly 53 million people before the war to about 17 million after, a drop sometimes cited as tens of millions of deaths — though historians caution the censuses also collapsed because the state lost the ability to count, not only because people died. An Lushan himself was enormously fat, reportedly a court favorite who could still perform a whirling 'barbarian' dance, and he didn't even outlast his own rebellion: he was murdered in 757 by his own son, who seized control of the revolt that still bears the father's name.

events.label: Seljuk Migration
events.description: Three centuries after the Türk collapse, the Seljuks — Turkic nomads who had taken up Sunni Islam — poured out of the Aral Sea region into Iran, smashed the Ghaznavid dynasty in 1040, and seized Baghdad in 1055. Their kin in the Sultanate of Rum then tore most of Anatolia away from Byzantium after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: They took their name from an ancestor, Seljuk ibn Duqaq, an Oghuz war-chief whose own father bore the nickname 'Iron Bow' for his skill as an archer. At Manzikert the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan did something rare: he captured the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV alive, then released him on terms — only for Romanos to return home, be deposed, and have his own court blind him, dying of the wounds. When Tughril Beg entered Baghdad the caliph crowned him 'Sultan,' a title that effectively reduced the once-supreme Abbasid caliph to a religious figurehead while the Turkic sultan held the real power.

events.label: Ottoman Founding
events.description: Around 1299 a minor frontier chief named Osman declared independence in northwestern Anatolia, founding the dynasty that bears his name. The Ottomans would go on to take Constantinople in 1453, conquer Egypt in 1517, twice besiege Vienna, and rule across three continents until 1922 — the longest-lived of all the post-Türk empires.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ottoman tradition traced the family to the Kayı clan of the Oghuz Turks, but many modern historians suspect that pedigree was invented later to dress up a humble warband with prestigious ancestry. Founding legend has the young Osman dreaming that a tree grew from his chest to shade the whole world, a vision his spiritual mentor Sheikh Edebali read as a prophecy of empire — though that tale was first written down roughly a century after Osman died. His tiny base was the town of Söğüt; from that speck the dynasty grew into a 600-year world power.

events.label: Modern Turkic Languages
events.description: Today's Turkic language family — over 200 million speakers from Turkey across Central Asia to Xinjiang and the Volga — descends from the speech first written down in the Orkhon Inscriptions. The very word 'Türk' as a people's name was the Ashina dynasty's invention: nobody used it before 552, and after 552 almost every Turkic-speaker eventually did.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The family runs to more than 40 distinct languages, and Turkish alone, with around 85 million speakers, accounts for nearly four in ten of all Turkic-speakers. They sort into neat branches whose names echo this very chapter — an Oghuz branch (Turkish, Azerbaijani, Turkmen) tracing to the Seljuk-Ottoman line, a Karluk branch (Uzbek, Uyghur) to the people who flipped at Talas, and a Kipchak branch (Kazakh, Tatar, Kyrgyz) to the western steppe nomads. The languages stayed close enough that a Turkish and an Azerbaijani speaker can still roughly follow each other, more than a thousand years after the dispersal began.

events.label: Khazar Khaganate
events.description: The Khazars, Turkic-speakers who split from the Western Türks in the 600s, built a trading empire on the Volga and the Caucasus that controlled the routes between the Byzantine, Muslim, and Viking worlds. Their royal court converted to Judaism around 740 — the only Jewish-ruled state outside ancient Israel — and they held off Arab expansion for two centuries until the Rus destroyed them in 969.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Much of what we think we know about the conversion comes from the 'Khazar Correspondence,' a set of tenth-century Hebrew letters supposedly exchanged between a Khazar king named Joseph and a Jewish minister of the Caliph of Córdoba in Spain — documents most scholars accept as genuine but which remain debated. Their capital, Atil, sat on the lower Volga near present-day Astrakhan in Russia, though its exact site has never been pinned down. The Khazars' reputation as a tolerant trade hub was real enough that legend has them weighing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam side by side before choosing the faith that bound them to neither of their giant neighbors.

events.label: Bulgars and Pechenegs
events.description: Two more Turkic peoples reshaped Europe. The Bulgars crossed the Danube under Asparuh in 680 and founded the First Bulgarian Empire, ruling a Slavic majority that gradually absorbed them. The Pechenegs later dominated the grasslands north of the Black Sea, beating Byzantine and Rus armies before the Cumans swallowed them in the 1100s.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Asparuh's victory at the Battle of Ongal in the Danube delta forced the Byzantine emperor Constantine IV to sign a treaty in 681 actually paying tribute to the new Bulgar state — the first time the empire formally recognized a barbarian kingdom on what it considered its own soil. The Pechenegs left an even grislier mark: in 972 their khan Kurya ambushed and killed the Rus prince Sviatoslav at the Dnieper rapids and, according to the Rus chronicle, had the prince's skull lined with gold and turned into a drinking cup — a trophy in the old steppe tradition.

events.label: Tian Shan and the Western Heartland
events.description: The Tian Shan ('Heavenly Mountains') range, running 1,500 miles from western China through Kyrgyzstan, was the geographic spine of the Western Türk Khaganate. Its high pastures fed Türk horse herds, its passes controlled the northern Silk Road, and its slopes hosted Istemi's court at Suyab in modern Kyrgyzstan. Zemarchus crossed the Tian Shan in 569 to reach Istemi and described the snow-capped peaks in detail.

events.label: Suyab
events.description: Suyab (SOO-yab) was the western capital of the Türk khaganate, located in the Chu River valley near modern Tokmok in Kyrgyzstan. It served Istemi as a base for his westward expansion, hosted Maniakh's mission to Constantinople in 568, received Zemarchus's return embassy in 569, and continued as a major Silk Road oasis under the Tang's Anxi Protectorate. The Tang poet Li Bai is supposed to have been born there.

events.label: Tarim Basin Oasis Kingdoms
events.description: The oasis kingdoms ringing the Taklamakan Desert in the Tarim Basin — Kashgar, Khotan, Kucha, Karashahr, Turfan, and Loulan — were the chain of stepping-stones along the Silk Road. They were variously Iranian (Sogdian), Tocharian-speaking (an extinct Indo-European language), and Buddhist before Türk and then Tang overlordship arrived. After 640 they came under Tang Anxi Protectorate control; after 751 they began their long conversion to Islam under Karluk and then Karakhanid rule.

events.label: Kucha and Kashgar
events.description: Kucha and Kashgar were the two anchor oases of the Tarim Basin — Kucha a wealthy Buddhist city on the northern rim, Kashgar the western gateway where the caravan roads climbed into the Pamirs. Both became Tang garrison towns under the Anxi Protectorate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Kucha's most famous son was the translator Kumarajiva (344-413), born to a Kuchean princess and an Indian monk; he was hauled off to China and produced the Chinese Buddhist translations that are still read today. Just outside Kucha sit the Kizil Caves, the oldest major Buddhist cave-temple complex in China — 236 cave shrines cut into a cliff, with murals painted between roughly the 3rd and 8th centuries that blend Indian, Persian, and even Roman artistic touches. Kashgar's ancient name was Shule, and it had been a Chinese outpost on and off since the Han general Ban Chao garrisoned it six centuries earlier.

events.label: Türk Rejection of Buddhism
events.description: Unlike most of the settled empires they brushed up against, the Türks largely refused to adopt Buddhism, sticking instead with Tengri sky worship and shamanic practice. Tonyukuk argued the choice was strategic: a religion that made men gentle would dull the warrior edge that kept the steppe ahead of its neighbors.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chinese sources record that the moment of decision was real: Bilge Kagan himself wanted to convert, build Buddhist temples, and put up walled cities, and it was Tonyukuk who talked him out of all three. He reportedly warned that Buddhism and Taoism breed "kindness and weakness" unfit for a people built on raiding and conquest, and that fixed temples would tie the Türks down and erase their customs. His prescription was that they should keep "following the water and the grass" — the nomad's seasonal migration between pastures.

events.label: Türk Shamanism (Kam)
events.description: Türk religious specialists, called kam, communicated with Tengri and the spirits through trance, drumming, and animal sacrifice. The English word 'shaman' reaches us from the Tungusic languages of Siberia, but the practice was the same one Türk kams performed for the khagans. Kams advised on marriage, war, and politics, performed funeral rites, and conducted purification ceremonies — Zemarchus described being purified by smoking branches before being admitted to Istemi's tent.

events.label: Otuken Mountain (Sacred Land)
events.description: The sacred upland of Türk belief — never pinned to an exact peak, somewhere in the Khangai highlands around the Orkhon — held to be the one place from which a khagan could legitimately rule all the Turkic tribes.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Türks believed a divine force called 'qut' (roughly, heavenly fortune or charisma) radiated from Ötüken and granted whoever held it the right to command. Scholars think the sacred zone stretched from the Khangai Range down toward the Sayan Mountains of Tuva, with the Orkhon Valley at its center, today straddling Mongolia's Arkhangai and Övörkhangai provinces. The eighth-century stone inscriptions put the doctrine bluntly: stay in the Ötüken land and send your caravans out from there, and you will rule the tribes forever — wander off, and you are finished.

events.label: Yenisei Kyrgyz
events.description: The Kyrgyz, a Türk-speaking people of the upper Yenisei basin in southern Siberia, paid intermittent tribute to the Türk khaganate but were never fully subjugated. After the Türk collapse they remained a regional power, eventually destroying the Uyghur Khaganate in 840 and briefly dominating the Mongolian steppe before being driven back to the Yenisei by the Khitan. They are the ancestors of the modern Kyrgyz people of Central Asia.

events.label: Rise of the Khitan
events.description: The Khitan, a Para-Mongolic-speaking people in eastern Mongolia and Manchuria, were Türk subjects in the seventh century but emerged as an independent power after the Türk collapse. They would eventually found the Liao Dynasty in 916, ruling northern China and the Mongolian steppe for two centuries. The Khitan name became the European word 'Cathay' for China, transmitted through medieval Russian.

events.label: Tibetan Empire as Türk Rival
events.description: As the eastern Türks sat under Tang rule, a brand-new heavyweight rose on the plateau to the south: the Tibetan Empire, which began clawing the Silk Road oases away from the Tang in the 660s and 670s.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The turning point was the Battle of Dafei River in 670, where a Tang army was routed — the worst Chinese defeat in the region in decades. Tibet promptly seized all Four Garrisons of Anxi and held them until the Tang fought their way back in 692. This was no longer the small mountain kingdom of Songtsen Gampo (who had died around 650); under his successors Tibet became a plateau-spanning empire that would briefly sack the Tang capital itself in 763. The three-cornered fight over the Tarim — Tang, Tibet, and Türk fragments — dragged on for well over a century.

events.label: Avars in Europe
events.description: The Avars, who built a steppe empire on the Hungarian plain in the 560s and menaced Byzantium for two centuries, may have been the western remnants of the Rouran fleeing the Türk revolt — though scholars still argue the point.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Recent DNA studies of Avar-era graves in the Carpathian Basin have found genetic links to populations of the Mongolian steppe, lending support to the old idea that the Avar elite came from there — without fully settling whether they were specifically Rouran. Their migration was startlingly fast, covering thousands of miles across Eurasia in roughly a decade. The empire they founded under Khagan Bayan lasted until Charlemagne's Franks broke it apart in 796, and it was through Avar warriors that the iron stirrup first reached Western Europe.

events.label: The Türk Purification Ceremony
events.description: Before Zemarchus could even meet the khagan in 569, the Türks ran his whole embassy through a fire-purification rite — shamans circling the Byzantines' baggage with burning incense, beating drums, and ringing bells to chase off evil spirits.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Menander's description is unusually concrete: the Türks made the envoys pass between two fires, carried flaming leaves around their luggage while chanting in what he called 'Scythian,' and only then let them approach. Diplomacy aside, it was a genuine religious safeguard — outsiders were treated as spiritually contaminated and had to be cleansed before nearing the sacred space around the khagan. Because so little sixth-century steppe ritual was ever written down by literate observers, this passage is one of the richest surviving snapshots of early Türk shamanic practice.

events.label: Tonyukuk Inscription
events.description: The Tonyukuk inscription, erected near the Tula River around 720 during Tonyukuk's lifetime, is the earliest of the three Orkhon Inscriptions and the only one whose subject lived to oversee its carving. In it, Tonyukuk — by then over seventy and the elder statesman of the Second Khaganate — narrates his role in the 682 revolt and the rebuilding of the Türk state. The first-person voice is unusually direct and unmediated by court flattery.

events.label: Bilge Kagan Inscription
events.description: Erected in 735 a year after Bilge's death, the Bilge Kagan inscription is the longest and most political of the three Orkhon Inscriptions. It contains Bilge's own statements about his reign, his brother Kul Tigin's death, and his programmatic warning to future Türks not to be seduced by Chinese gifts and titles. Together with the Kul Tigin and Tonyukuk inscriptions, it forms the core of what we know about the Second Khaganate from a Türk rather than Chinese perspective.

events.label: Thomsen's Decipherment
events.description: The Old Turkic script of the Orkhon Inscriptions was not deciphered until 1893, when the Danish philologist Vilhelm Thomsen cracked the system in a single intense week of work, identifying it as a Turkic language related to modern Uyghur and Kazakh. The decipherment opened the entire Türk literary tradition to modern scholarship and confirmed that what had looked like Germanic-style runes was in fact a custom alphabet adapted from Sogdian.
